30: So a batch fixed at the start runs at the pace of its slowest member. The three strategies are three answers to that, in increasing order of how much they do about it.
32: The simplest answer does nothing about it. Collect a fixed number of requests, run them together, and return everything when the last one finishes.

34: R3 stops generating at t=9 and sits on the GPU until t=15, because R2 is still running. That costs you twice:
35: Six units of latency for a user whose answer was already done
36: A held slot that a queued request could have used
37: Waste scales with higher output variance. Anyscale measured this on OPT-13B on a 40GB A100. Widening the spread of output lengths dropped static batching to roughly 81 tokens per second, while continuous batching held an order of magnitude higher.
38: Still the right call sometimes. Static batching only looks bad when output lengths vary. Take that away and the slow-member problem goes with it.
39: Classification, embeddings, and scoring do exactly that. Each emits a fixed-size output, a label or a vector, so every request in the batch finishes at nearly the same step and none waits on a straggler.
40: For that kind of work, static batching is simpler and gives up nothing.

42: llm.generate hands the engine the whole workload at once. Cap max_tokens, keep prompt sizes similar, and every sequence finishes at nearly the same step.
43: 👉 The Hugging Face pipeline API with a batch_size argument is also static batching. Fine for evaluation scripts, poor for live traffic.
45: Static batching has a second cost. A request can wait a long time just to enter a batch.
46: If the batch size is 8 and only 5 have arrived, those 5 sit idle until three more show up.
47: Dynamic batching adds a timer. The batch fires on the size limit or when the window expires, whichever comes first.
48: Here's how the end state looks like:
49: Batch 1 fires at t=4 (the fixed interval) with only R1 and R2, because the window expired before a third arrived. Both start four units earlier than static batching allowed.
50: It shortens the wrong wait. R1 finishes at t=7 and still waits until t=12, because R2 is not done.
51: Dynamic batching decides once per batch, then hands control to the engine until every member is done. For fixed-output models that is a complete answer, which is why Triton ships it.
52: 👉 preferred_batch_size lists the sizes the scheduler tries to form. max_queue_delay_microseconds caps how long a request waits for company.
54: Both strategies so far treat a batch as one unit of work that starts and runs until every request in the batch has finished. That assumption is what still costs you, and continuous batching drops it.
55: The scheduler runs one iteration, gets control back, and decides again. The moment a sequence emits its final token it leaves the batch, and a waiting request takes that slot on the next pass.
56: The batch composition changes every iteration, which is why this is iteration-level scheduling. No slot waits for the slowest sequence, so the GPU stays saturated even when output lengths vary wildly.

58: The limit is memory, not compute. Every active sequence holds a KV cache that grows with each token, and that cache, not the math, is what caps how many sequences fit.
59: On a 40GB A100 with a 13B model resident, only a handful of long sequences fit at once. When the pool runs out, the scheduler evicts a running request and recomputes it later.
